prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep a single prize part on B043 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and my configuration has not changed. What has changed is how I hold it. The six round-1 files agree on the scientific case, so I no longer treat that agreement as an argument. The argument stands on the discovery itself: proglucagon processing and the human incretin effect, identification of the truncated active peptide, and its receptor biology all precede the long-acting agonists. The clinical consequence of that chain is documented in large independent outcome trials, with benefit in type 2 diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. The discovery changed both a research field and clinical practice. It is mature, not premature, and the mechanism has stayed stable under decades of testing. Holst and Drucker are secure. The third place is a judgement between two defensible readings. I think Mojsov is the better fit for a prize that recognises discoveries rather than a drug programme, and I would want the citation to say so.
statement.case_against: The attribution weakness remains and I cannot remove it from the supplied text. Mojsov's priority for identifying the active GLP-1 form is described as contested against Habener and colleagues, who are not credited. If primary evidence showed that her role was not independent or not first, the third place would be hard to defend and the configuration would need to be reopened. Omitting Knudsen can also be read as honouring the biology while leaving out the step that produced liraglutide and semaglutide. A citation framed on physiology risks sounding evasive about that omission. Finally, a three-name GLP-1 prize uses the whole allocation and leaves no room for a second achievement such as the unfolded protein response, which has a cleaner two-name credit and is arguably as overdue.

responses.point: Svenningsson reports moving from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen at opening to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, so that the prize rests on physiology and the active peptide rather than on industrial analogue design.
responses.response: In round 1 I described your trio as still including Knudsen, which your file corrects, and I am glad the chair has the position right. We now agree on the names and the reasoning. I want to stay honest about what that reasoning does and does not establish. Preferring discovery over development is a principle, not evidence that Mojsov's priority is secure. You reached your position partly because Mojsov's credit is a problem for you, as it is for me, and I would not let two members moving to the same trio hide that the priority question is untested in the supplied text. I accept your question in the chair's summary that if her priority fails scrutiny, the committee must say why she is the name omitted rather than Knudsen, and I would reopen the third place on primary-literature grounds, not on any count of support.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks the unfolded protein response first for mechanistic originality and clean two-name attribution, and worries that GLP-1 is almost too obvious and may push aside an equally overdue discovery.
responses.response: Your point that obviousness should not be a reason to hesitate is fair, and it also cuts the other way: obviousness is not a reason to rank GLP-1 lower, and opening support should not decide this. The decisive difference for me is consequence. The unfolded protein response is original and complete as a pathway, but its human-disease links to diabetes, neurodegeneration and cancer remain largely conceptual, and the credit for the PERK, ATF6 and integrated stress response arms lies partly outside Walter and Mori, so its allocation is less clean than it looks. I keep B032 as my first alternative and would take it seriously as the leading candidate for a later year if GLP-1 is awarded. I do not agree that a single GLP-1 prize must be split to make room for it, since the three-person limit would then force a weaker allocation on both.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius frames the choice as physiology only versus including industrial drug development, and in her file settles on Drucker, Holst and Mojsov with Knudsen omitted, while holding CAR-T or cGAS-STING as later candidates.
responses.response: In round 1 I treated you as naming Knudsen, which your file does not do, so I correct that. Your framing of the physiology-versus-development question is the right one, and I resolve it in favour of physiology while accepting your point that this makes the omission something the citation must own. I like the wording in your citation that names both the physiology and the active form. On your later-year question I rank CAR-T ahead of cGAS-STING. cGAS-STING is early on therapeutic translation, as you and Sandberg note. CAR-T has clinical proof but the credit gap around Eshhar's original chimeric receptor concept is real, so I would not call it ready to allocate without a different or enlarged name list.

responses.point: Linnarsson says an unresolved priority dispute is a reason to examine the primary literature rather than to default to a cleaner alternative, and accepts that he relies on recollection of the historical record.
responses.response: I agree, and you should hold me to the same standard. I am also relying on recollection of the Mojsov and Habener history, and none of us can claim to have settled it. Because the supplied text does not resolve it, the honest position is that Mojsov is the more defensible third name on the evidence we have, not a proven one. I do not want to switch to B032 merely because its attribution is tidy, as that would substitute convenience for judgement on a discovery that matters more. I would apply the test you suggest: if credible primary evidence showed that Habener's group identified the active form independently and first, I would revisit the trio rather than leave the field.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1 peptide is secure enough to carry a laureate place, given the Habener dispute; the supplied text cannot settle it and I rely on recollection for the history.
Whether leaving out Knudsen, and framing the citation on physiology, will be read as principled or as evasive; this depends on how clearly the citation separates discovery from drug development.
Whether CAR-T (B019) can be allocated fairly without Eshhar, and which of B032, B019 or B013 should be held as the leading candidate if GLP-1 is awarded.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B043, B032 or B019. My nuclear-receptor and dopamine-neuron research, and my earlier co-authorship with Ronald Evans, do not involve any credited name on these ballots. For transparency, I have about twenty co-authored works with Per Svenningsson and one 2009 paper with Abdel El Manira, as the chair summary also records. None of them is credited on a shortlisted ballot, and I do not treat this as requiring recusal. Shared Karolinska affiliation is not treated as a conflict.
